routes.description: Establish traditional responsibility for the canonical Gospels by combining early attribution traditions with internal features linking each work to its named author or apostolic source.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the combined external and internal evidence makes Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John, including authorship under their authority, the most reasonable identities behind the canonical works.

motionBridge.description: Connect the four canonical texts to Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John either as writers or as controlling apostolic authorities behind their production.

centralBridges.description: Show that the early attribution tradition is sufficiently early, geographically broad, and continuous to preserve genuine authorial knowledge.
Show that internal narrative, eyewitness, linguistic, and biographical features fit the traditionally identified authors or their sources.
Show that literary dependence, Greek composition, and possible assistance are compatible with responsibility by the traditional figures.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Explain why the comparatively less prominent names Mark and Luke are unlikely selections for a purely prestige-driven fabrication.
Apply standards for anonymous ancient works and delayed attribution consistently when assessing the Gospel traditions.

routes.description: Establish anonymous later authorship by showing that secure traditional attributions arise late, that alternative diffusion explains their unanimity, and that the named figures do not fit the texts' production.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the evidence does not adequately identify the traditional figures as writers or controlling authorities and a later naming process better explains the surviving attributions.

motionBridge.description: Show that the canonical texts cannot be historically connected with sufficient specificity to authorship by or under the authority of the four traditional figures.

centralBridges.description: Establish a material chronological gap between Gospel composition and unambiguous attribution of the surviving canonical texts.
Establish that the traditional apostolic figures lacked the education and literary capacity required to compose the sophisticated Greek narratives.
Explain the stable fourfold naming tradition through a later authority-conferring origin and subsequent dissemination rather than independent authorial memory.
Distinguish an underlying witness or source from the final literary author and require evidence identifying the latter with a traditional figure.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Test whether Papias, Justin, and later witnesses identify the canonical works reliably and independently.
Determine whether ancient secretarial practices support delegation of long-form Greek narrative composition in another person's name.

sections.title: Timing and continuity of external attribution
sections.rationale: The timing, independence, and geographical spread of the naming tradition determine whether it transmits authorial knowledge or reflects a convention established after the texts circulated.

sections.title: Explanation for the traditional names
sections.rationale: Competing explanations for why these four names became stable bear directly on whether unanimity reflects inherited knowledge or an authority-conferring attribution process.

sections.title: Literacy, Greek composition, and delegated production
sections.rationale: The motion requires determining whether the traditional figures could be responsible for the canonical Greek narratives, including whether assistance can bridge the asserted educational and literary mismatch.

sections.title: Internal identification of Mark and Luke
sections.rationale: The proposed links between Mark and Peter and between Luke-Acts and a companion of Paul are central text-specific steps in extending traditional responsibility beyond the apostolic names.

sections.title: Internal identification of Matthew and John
sections.rationale: Matthew and John supply the principal apostolic identifications at issue, requiring assessment of whether internal features identify those disciples or only sources and conventionally named literary authors.

moves.speaker: Michael Licona
moves.proposition: Early and geographically diverse Christian testimony consistently attributes the canonical Gospels to Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John, with some testimony linked to companions of apostles.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly gives Licona the floor at event 49, and this uninterrupted opening presentation continues through event 211.

response.rationale: This constructive opening directly advances the external-attribution bridge by presenting early, geographically dispersed, and consistent testimony for all four traditional names.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It is a focused constructive contribution addressing a central route, though the independence and exact identification of the witnesses remain compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claimed evidential pattern and its scope are clear, but the limits of dependence among witnesses and the meaning of early are left implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Six sources and geographic spread support a serious cumulative case, but unanimity and proximity alone do not establish independence or exact canonical identification.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from early, widespread agreement to preserved authorial knowledge is intelligible, with dependence as one bounded missing bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move identifies multiple witnesses and regions, but their dates, independence, and precise reference to the canonical texts require further defense.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The testimony directly supports the central external-evidence bridge and covers the complete fourfold attribution pattern.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move principally states a constructive evidential case rather than materially representing a developed opposing explanation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt invokes six sources within fifteen to one hundred years of the final Gospel and lists Judea, Asia Minor, Gaul, Egypt, and Rome.

moves.speaker: Michael Licona
moves.proposition: Mark's prominence of Peter, portrayal of Peter's personality, and preservation of Aramaic sayings fit the claim that Mark recorded material derived from Peter.
moves.attributionBasis: This passage remains within Licona's uninterrupted opening statement after he expressly turns from external to internal evidence.

response.rationale: This constructive move advances the internal-identification bridge by connecting Peter's narrative prominence and characterization in Mark with a Petrine source behind the text.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It supplies concrete internal observations, but the inference from narrative prominence to source identity is only briefly defended.

precisionFindings.rationale: The Petrine-source claim and cited features are clear, while the distinction between compatibility and positive identification remains implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Peter's prominence is compatible with Petrine influence, but other literary explanations for prominence are not compared before drawing the source inference.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The route is intelligible, but the move leaves a material bridge between a character's prominence and the identity of an authorial source.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The quantified prominence supplies relevant textual support, though the personality and Aramaic evidence and rival literary explanations remain underdeveloped.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move materially supports the internal-evidence bridge for Mark, but it addresses only one of the four Gospel identifications.

representationalCharity.rationale: No developed alternative account of Peter's narrative prominence is represented closely enough for a meaningful charity test.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt states that Peter appears in nineteen of twenty-one named-disciple encounters and is frequently the sole disciple interacting with Jesus.

moves.speaker: Michael Licona
moves.proposition: The first-person plural travel narratives in Acts indicate participation by a companion of Paul, and external testimony makes Luke the most reasonable identification of that companion-author.
moves.attributionBasis: The passage is part of Licona's continuous opening and begins with his explicit transition from the internal evidence for Mark to Luke.

response.rationale: This constructive move advances internal identification by linking Acts' first-person plural travel passages to a Pauline companion and then identifying Luke through external testimony.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It gives a clear two-stage identification route, though the inference that the we narrator participated personally is not defended against alternatives.

precisionFindings.rationale: The companion-author inference and Luke identification are recoverable, with alternative literary uses of first-person narration left as an implicit qualification.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The combination of travel narration and tradition supports plausibility, but it does not by itself uniquely select Luke from Paul's coworkers.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The argument has a coherent two-step structure, but personal participation and the exclusion of other companions remain material implicit bridges.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Acts and Pauline coworker lists are relevant evidence, while the claimed unanimity and uniqueness of Luke need comparative substantiation.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the central internal-identification bridge with a text-specific argument for Luke-Acts.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move does not expressly reconstruct a developed rival explanation of the first-person plural passages.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt invokes the we narratives, roughly a dozen traveling coworkers, Luke's appearance in three letters, and unanimous external attribution.

moves.speaker: Michael Licona
moves.proposition: The Fourth Gospel presents an eyewitness source identified as the beloved disciple, whose access and place among the named disciples make John son of Zebedee the best candidate.
moves.attributionBasis: Licona explicitly transitions to John within the same uninterrupted opening statement, with no speaker change before the passage concludes.

response.rationale: This constructive argument identifies the beloved disciple by narrowing the candidates present in John 21 and appealing to access associated with Jesus' inner circle.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The elimination argument is explicit and directly relevant, though it does not fully establish that the eyewitness source was the final literary author.

precisionFindings.rationale: The candidate-elimination claim is clear, but the source-versus-final-writer distinction remains an important implicit qualification.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The narrowing makes John a plausible candidate, but assumptions about the beloved disciple's membership, James's exclusion, and literary authorship remain contestable.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The eliminative structure is stable, but it depends on the beloved disciple belonging to the specified inner circle and being authorially controlling.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The named group, access, and chronological exclusion are concrete evidence, but the crucial identification and authorship warrants remain compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supports a central internal-identification bridge for one of the two apostolic names most important to the motion.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move develops its own candidate analysis without representing a sufficiently specific competing identification or source-author distinction.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt lists the seven disciples, distinguishes Peter, excludes James by early martyrdom, and identifies John as the remaining inner-circle candidate.

moves.speaker: Michael Licona
moves.proposition: Matthew's fiscal and Jewish features, together with early tradition, support Matthew's substantial involvement in a Greek Gospel produced from earlier Semitic material and Mark.
moves.attributionBasis: This is Licona's final Gospel-specific argument in his opening, introduced by an explicit transition to Matthew and followed by his overall conclusion.

response.rationale: This constructive move principally advances the production bridge by proposing substantial Matthean involvement through earlier Semitic material, Markan use, Greek composition, and supervision.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It offers a production model responsive to literary dependence, but the model's historical basis and exact division of labor remain underdeveloped.

precisionFindings.rationale: Substantial involvement is recoverable but flexible, and the relation among an Aramaic collection, Greek composition, supervision, and final authorship is not sharply delimited.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The Josephus analogy establishes possibility, but the proposed lost Semitic collection and supervised Greek production need independent evidence to support probability.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The production scenario is internally possible, but several distinct claims are joined without a defended bridge from compatibility to actual Matthean responsibility.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Markan dependence and added material are relevant facts, while the lost Semitic source and supervised Greek edition carry substantial speculative weight.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move materially advances the central production bridge and bears directly on how Matthew could remain responsible for the Greek Gospel.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move constructs a harmonizing production proposal without sufficiently stating a developed opposing account of Matthew's literary dependence.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says the Greek author used Mark, added about forty-four percent, and compares a lost Semitic precursor with Josephus's supervised Greek work.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.proposition: The canonical Gospels circulated without self-identification, and the first unambiguous attribution of the surviving four texts to their traditional authors appears roughly a century later.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator transition and Ehrman's opening remarks identify him as the speaker, and the passage is an uninterrupted portion of his opening statement.

components.text: Whether the cited testimony securely and unambiguously attributes the surviving canonical four before the late second century.
Whether geographic spread and agreement demonstrate independent preservation rather than later diffusion.

response.rationale: The reply directly contests the alleged earliness by dating the first unambiguous fourfold attribution around 185, but it does not yet answer the separate independence and diffusion warrant.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive chronology component strongly while leaving the geographic-independence component substantially unanswered in this span.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move specifies canonical texts, approximate dates, and the narrower standard of unambiguous attribution, while acknowledging that composition dates can be disputed.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The asserted chronological gap fits the supplied conventional dating and is qualified by acknowledging possible disagreement over exact Gospel dates.

charity.alternative: Earlier testimony may preserve traditional attribution even if the surviving references are not fully explicit about the canonical texts.
charity.decisiveQualification: The reply distinguishes possible earlier allusions from the first unambiguous attribution of the surviving four canonical works.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move supplies conventional date ranges and a precise attribution benchmark, though fuller treatment of Papias and Justin would strengthen verification.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central attribution-gap bridge and attacks the claimed earliness of the external case.

representationalCharity.rationale: It preserves the possibility of disputed earlier evidence while focusing its criticism on the narrower and stronger claim of secure identification.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt dates Mark around 70, Matthew and Luke around 80–85, John around 90–95, and the earliest unambiguous attributions around 185.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.proposition: Galilean disciples lacking elite Greek literary education could not plausibly have composed the sophisticated Greek narratives preserved as the canonical Gospels.
moves.attributionBasis: The passage remains in Ehrman's uninterrupted opening statement and is introduced as his most important consideration about the authors' identities.

components.text: Whether identifying an eyewitness source as John establishes that John possessed or controlled the literary capacity producing the final Greek Gospel.
Whether a proposed Semitic precursor and supervised Greek version adequately bridge Matthew's educational and compositional limitations.

response.rationale: The move supplies powerful contrary material about educational capacity but does not directly engage the pro side's distinct source, supervision, or under-authority production mechanisms.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The literacy evidence is highly issue-bearing, yet it leaves the decisive assisted-production and source-versus-writer components uncontacted.

precisionFindings.rationale: The educational mismatch is clear, but the move shifts from Peter and John to all relevant disciples and from personal composition to any possible responsibility.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Evidence of ordinary Galilean literacy makes direct sophisticated Greek composition unlikely, but cannot establish impossibility without addressing later education, collaborators, or delegated production.

charity.alternative: Traditional responsibility may involve sources, later-acquired competence, translators, or assistants rather than unaided autograph composition.
charity.decisiveQualification: The reply establishes a serious default educational mismatch but does not separately exclude those under-authority production models.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The mismatch inference is intelligible, but the categorical conclusion exceeds premises about typical education and leaves alternative production mechanisms unresolved.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Acts 4:13 and social-literacy considerations provide substantial support, though one term and population generalizations bear more weight than fully demonstrated.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move squarely supports the central con literacy bridge and poses a major challenge to direct apostolic composition.

representationalCharity.rationale: Its formulation that no follower could possibly have composed the works weakens the broader traditional position by treating direct personal composition as exhaustive.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt cites Acts 4:13's description of Peter and John as unlettered and contrasts Galilean disciples with sophisticated Greek narrative composition.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.proposition: The traditional names were plausibly assigned late to give four previously anonymous church Gospels apostolic authority against rival writings bearing authoritative names.

components.text: Whether early and geographically diverse attribution is better explained by preserved authorial knowledge than by a later common naming origin.

response.rationale: The move gives a directly contrary late-naming explanation, but it does not contact the pro move's evidentiary premise concerning the actual dates, locations, and continuity of its witnesses.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It presents a pertinent rival hypothesis with an intelligible motive, but does not compare that hypothesis against the cited early testimony.

precisionFindings.rationale: The late authority-conferring hypothesis is clearly recoverable, though the agents, location, and timing of the naming act remain implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The authority incentive makes late naming plausible, but motive and natural name choices do not establish that this process actually generated the fourfold tradition.

charity.alternative: Stable fourfold attribution may transmit inherited knowledge rather than result from strategic authority-conferring invention.
charity.decisiveQualification: The reply offers an incentive for naming but does not explain the pro side's claimed early and geographically distributed attestations.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The proposed incentive-to-naming inference is coherent, but the move lacks intermediate evidence connecting the general authority contest to these particular attributions.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Anonymous church books and rival apostolic titles form relevant context, while the decisive historical naming event is largely reconstructed rather than evidenced.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly advances the central alternative-origin bridge by supplying a mechanism and motive for later attribution.

representationalCharity.rationale: It reduces the traditional case to institutional need without confronting its strongest claimed evidence of early continuity and geographic spread.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt argues that anonymous church Gospels faced rival writings bearing apostolic names, creating pressure to assign Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John.

moves.speaker: Michael Licona
moves.proposition: Anonymous composition and delayed explicit attribution do not defeat traditional authorship because comparable ancient works rely on similarly late testimony, while Papias and Justin provide earlier support for Mark.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly awards Licona the first rebuttal at event 395, and Licona identifies the opposing claims he is reviewing throughout this passage.

components.text: Whether anonymous composition and a long delay before unambiguous attribution make traditional authorship historically inadequate.
Whether Papias and Justin unambiguously identify the surviving canonical texts rather than related traditions or other writings.

response.rationale: The reply contests the inference from anonymity and delay through comparative ancient practice and advances Papias and Justin as earlier Markan evidence, contacting both chronology and identification.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It answers the principal inferential demand and offers earlier witnesses, though the canonical identification and comparability warrants remain contested.

precisionFindings.rationale: The rebuttal's comparative and witness-based claims are clear, while the conditions making other anonymous works genuinely comparable remain implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Comparative practice and earlier testimony weaken a simple argument from silence, but do not by themselves show that Papias and Justin identify canonical Mark securely.

charity.alternative: The decisive issue is not mere anonymity but the absence of unambiguous attribution of these surviving texts until roughly a century later.
charity.decisiveQualification: The rebuttal recognizes the delay but treats comparable ancient attribution and disputed earlier Markan testimony as reasons it is not defeating.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The move validly shows that anonymity and delay are not automatically defeating, but its positive traditional conclusion still depends on disputed witness identification.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Comparable ancient works, Papias, and Justin are relevant evidence, though the comparison class and the witnesses' reference to canonical Mark require fuller support.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central con attribution-gap bridge and bears strongly on the external-evidence route.

representationalCharity.rationale: It addresses the con argument in a materially accurate form, though the special force of unambiguous canonical identification receives limited development.

moves.evidenceBasis: The span reviews the external case against Ehrman's objections, invoking comparable delayed ancient attributions and earlier support from Papias and Justin.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.proposition: Justin's language and textual agreements are better explained by his use of the Gospel of Peter than by an attribution of canonical Mark to Peter.
moves.attributionBasis: The cross-examination sequence explicitly identifies Licona as questioner and Ehrman as the respondent giving this sustained answer.

components.text: Whether Justin's memoirs of Peter provide early evidence linking canonical Mark with Peter.
Whether internal Petrine features independently support Peter as the source behind canonical Mark.

response.rationale: The reply directly disputes the Justin component by identifying his terminology and textual agreements with the Gospel of Peter, but it does not answer Mark's internal features.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive Justin-identification issue with a specific alternative, while leaving the separate internal Petrine case untouched.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claim that Justin used the Gospel of Peter rather than canonical Mark is clear, though the extent and exclusivity of the textual agreement remain implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Terminology and verbatim agreements are relevant discriminating evidence, but the excerpt does not display enough comparison to establish the alternative decisively.

charity.alternative: Justin's memoir of Peter may refer to canonical Mark understood as recording Peter's recollections.
charity.decisiveQualification: The reply argues that Justin's wording and direct textual agreements point instead to the distinct Gospel of Peter.

logicalCoherence.rationale: If Justin's distinctive wording and agreements align uniquely with the Gospel of Peter, the proposed identification follows by a coherent comparative inference.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move identifies scholarly and textual grounds, but the selected span only begins the promised two-part demonstration and provides limited examples.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the witness-quality subsidiary bridge and materially weakens one proposed early link between Mark and Peter.

representationalCharity.rationale: It accurately states the Mark-based interpretation and answers it with a specific textual alternative rather than dismissing it by assertion.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt contrasts the proposal that Justin meant canonical Mark with Justin's phrase memoir of Peter and claimed verbatim agreements with another text.

moves.speaker: Michael Licona
moves.proposition: Christians inventing prestigious Gospel attributions would not plausibly have selected the comparatively less marketable Mark and Luke instead of direct disciples.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator-designated questioning sequence and the explicit turn-taking make Licona's identity as the speaker unambiguous.

components.text: Whether an authority-conferring fabrication would plausibly select the comparatively minor non-eyewitness names Mark and Luke.
Whether Matthew and John, together with Mark and Luke, form a coherent strategically authoritative fourfold set.

response.rationale: The reply directly challenges the name-choice plausibility of the late-fabrication hypothesis, but does not address the authority supplied by the four names as an integrated set.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts an important name-choice component with a comparative observation, while leaving the broader institutional mechanism and fourfold pattern unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The comparative marketability claim is clear, although what motives besides maximal prestige might govern fabricated attribution remains implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Later prestigious pseudonyms create a useful comparison, but fabricators could value links to Peter and Paul or continuity with existing traditions.

charity.alternative: Mark and Luke could be strategically useful because they connect the Gospels to Peter and Paul without claiming direct apostolic composition.
charity.decisiveQualification: The move asks why fabricators seeking maximum authority would nevertheless forgo more famous direct disciples used in later apocrypha.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The expectation that prestige-seeking invention favors prominent apostles is reasonable, but it is probabilistic and depends on a simplified model of name selection.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The comparison with later apocryphal names is relevant, though no base rate or fuller sample establishes that prestige was the only likely consideration.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the dedicated subsidiary name-choice bridge with a focused challenge to the fabrication hypothesis.

representationalCharity.rationale: It fairly identifies the prestige rationale but underrepresents the alternative strategic value of apostolic companions and a balanced fourfold witness.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt contrasts Mark and Luke with more marketable figures such as Peter, James, Thomas, and Mary found in later apocryphal Gospel titles.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.proposition: Mark and Luke were useful attribution choices because they were understood as companions of Peter and Paul, completing a representation of principal apostolic witness.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator invites an answer immediately after Licona's question, and the content is Ehrman's direct response within his established turn.

components.text: Whether Mark and Luke were too minor to serve the authority-conferring purposes of a fabricated attribution scheme.
Whether later apocryphal preference for direct disciples makes companion attributions historically unlikely.

response.rationale: The reply directly explains the authority value of Mark and Luke through Peter and Paul and the resulting complete apostolic witness, while not addressing the apocryphal comparison.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive inference about minor names with a concrete counter-explanation, leaving only the supporting comparative example unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The strategic reason for selecting two disciples and two apostolic companions is explicit, and its scope is confined to explaining the name set.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Tertullian's stated apostolic-link rationale directly supports the claim that Mark and Luke were useful rather than anomalous choices.

charity.alternative: Prestige-seeking fabricators should prefer direct disciples over comparatively minor Mark and Luke.
charity.decisiveQualification: Mark and Luke carried derivative authority as companions of Peter and Paul and completed a deliberately representative apostolic set.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The companion links directly answer the alleged anomaly and coherently explain how all four names could form a strategically authoritative set.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The appeal to Tertullian's own explanation is specific and apt, though it does not independently prove that this rationale caused the original naming.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly attacks the subsidiary name-choice bridge at its decisive premise concerning Mark and Luke's supposed lack of authority value.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply preserves the challenge's prestige premise while showing why the allegedly minor names could satisfy it indirectly.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt links Mark with Peter and Luke with Paul and cites Tertullian's rationale that the four names represent the principal apostolic witness.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.proposition: Matthew's references to taxes and money do not identify its author as a tax collector, because thematic vocabulary is not reliable evidence of an author's occupation.
moves.attributionBasis: Ehrman is the moderator-designated questioner and advances the comparison, while Licona's short answers are clearly distinguishable in the exchange.

components.text: Whether Matthew's greater attention to taxes and money is probative evidence that its author was a tax collector.
Whether early tradition and the proposed Semitic-to-Greek production history independently support Matthew's involvement.

response.rationale: The exchange directly tests and rejects the occupational inference from financial vocabulary, but it leaves the tradition and proposed production history untouched.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts one concrete internal feature effectively, while the broader multi-part Matthean identification argument remains unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move clearly distinguishes consistency with tax-collector authorship from evidence that makes such authorship more probable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The limited conclusion that thematic vocabulary does not reliably identify occupation fits the comparative questioning used to expose the weak inference.

charity.alternative: Matthew's relatively frequent references to taxes and money are consistent with and modestly support a tax-collector author.
charity.decisiveQualification: Consistency is not occupational identification, since subject vocabulary can reflect narrative content rather than the author's profession.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The comparative questioning exposes the warrant problem, though a broader linguistic analysis would be needed to establish the feature's complete evidential insignificance.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks a stated internal-identification consideration for Matthew, though only one component of that central bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply preserves the modest consistency claim while correctly focusing criticism on any stronger inference to authorial occupation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt elicits the claim that Matthew mentions taxes more than other Gospels and tests whether that frequency genuinely makes tax-collector authorship likelier.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.proposition: Later authorship witnesses are not independent once a naming tradition begins, and John's closing distinction between the beloved disciple and a collective authorial voice weighs against direct Johannine authorship.
moves.attributionBasis: Licona's rebuttal ends before this response, and the moderator's transition plus the first-person counterargument clearly identify Ehrman as speaker.

components.text: Whether identifying the beloved disciple as an eyewitness source also identifies him as the final Gospel's literary author.
Whether geographically dispersed later witnesses are independent evidence once a common naming tradition has begun.

response.rationale: The reply contacts both the source-versus-writer distinction in John's ending and the independence of later external witnesses after a naming tradition begins.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It answers two decisive components with targeted counterarguments, though the excerpt supplies more detail for witness dependence than for the closing grammar.

components.text: Whether later universal agreement and geographic spread independently establish that the traditional names accompanied the Gospels from composition.
Whether Justin's failure to use the four traditional names is compatible with an already established early attribution tradition.
